Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-29
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Recording link: https://redwood-recordings.example/ff-20281129-conflux-9b72

Summary (auto): Conflux is migrating several internal LLM features from a mix of managed APIs and a small internal inference fleet. They need a path to start with Hosted, move to Dedicated with reserved pools, and eventually evaluate a Private VPC deployment for regulated customers. Heavy emphasis on LangChain/LlamaIndex compatibility, how to front with an internal gateway, and quota/observability granularity.

Topics covered: see topics list above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan with Redwood, i'm joined by priya and mateo from our team. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Evan Torres: good, thanks. lots to cover. i'm Evan, CTO at Conflux. we brought maya and raj and sofia for infra and security specifics.
[00:14] Jordan Lee: great, quick agenda: integration patterns, probes for langchain and llamaindex, gateway/proxy, quotas and obs hooks, then next steps. sound ok?
[00:22] Maya Chen: yep that's perfect. we basically need to figure out minimal friction path. we use LangChain in production for retrieval-augmented generation and also a custom LlamaIndex connector for our vector DB.
[00:34] Priya Nair: okay cool, are you running the vectors in-house or a managed vector DB? sorry quick q.
[00:39] Maya Chen: in-house — self-hosted milvus cluster, everything sits in our VPC. so data residency matters.
[00:45] Raj Patel: and we have peak concurrency around 1.2k concurrent requests, typical p95 latency target for gen endpoints is 350–450 ms.
[00:54] Mateo Alvarez: got it, that's really helpful. one immediate thing: for hosted we provide VPC peering/private endpoints so traffic can stay in your network — is that something you'd consider for the first phase?
[01:04] Evan Torres: yes, but we need to know KMS integration and whether keys ever leave our control. our security team won't approve otherwise.
[01:11] Sofia Rivera: right — SOC2 is fine, but we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs, plus role-based access for model deployments. can you speak to which of those are supported?
[01:20] Priya Nair: yes — we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated; hosted can be configured to use your KMS via an HSM-backed wrapper or bring-your-own-key (depending on plan). audit logs and model-level RBAC are in the Console; we'll share the security playbook after.
[01:35] Maya Chen: okay nice, that helps. now, on the SDK side, we use python-based LangChain. how invasive is the SDK change? do we have to rewrite prompts?
[01:45] Jordan Lee: not at all — our Python SDK mirrors the OpenAI style calls and LangChain has an official Redwood adapter (or community one) — we also have a sample repo. in most cases you swap the client initialization and point to the gateway. you'll get token-level cost headers in responses.
[01:58] Raj Patel: when you say gateway, are you talking about a redwood endpoint we hit, or do you have a sidecar we can run inside our VPC?
[02:06] Priya Nair: both. we offer a lightweight gateway sidecar (runs as a k8s DaemonSet or standalone container) that performs routing, local caching of prefixes, and enforces local quotas before hitting Redwood. alternatively you can hit Hosted endpoints via private link. the sidecar is what many customers use when they want tight network control and lower egress.
[02:27] Maya Chen: any differences in behavior between sidecar and hosted if we use batching and kv cache? like do you preserve KV cache semantics for llama-like models?
[02:36] Priya Nair: yes, the sidecar keeps a local KV cache compatible with our runtime's prefix caching. there's small divergence if you use very aggressive quantization profiles, but typical gen workloads behave the same. note: we sometimes see transcription of "kv" as "kay-vee" in older docs, ha.
[02:52] Evan Torres: ha. okay. about LangChain, our repo uses chains+agents and occasional function calling. do you support function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs?
[03:02] Jordan Lee: yes — function calling, streaming and structured outputs are supported. we also have observability hooks that attach run IDs to spans and propagate through the LangChain adapter, so you can correlate tokens with traces.
[03:15] Raj Patel: what's the recommended way to enforce per-tenant quotas? we have multi-tenant customers and need token-level billing and hard limits per tenant, with soft-burst allowance for thier premium plans.
[03:26] Priya Nair: we provide per-api-key quotas and per-tenant policy enforcement. Policies can be rate-based (reqs/sec), token-based (tokens/min), or budget-based (monthly token cap). for bursts you can configure a token burst pool attached to a plan that drains over time. the sidecar can enforce local hard caps and shard requests to dedicated pools.
[03:47] Maya Chen: how do you measure tokens across model variants? we sometimes switch between gpt-like and open-llama variants.
[03:55] Mateo Alvarez: we normalize token accounting per model family based on tokenizer mapping. so switching model variant will show an adjusted token multiplier in billing; we send both raw and normalized token counts in the usage webhook.
[04:07] Evan Torres: ok great. latency — you mentioned dedicated pools. our concern is maintaining p95 at scale. what's typical p95 on a dedicated 4-GPU pool?
[04:16] Priya Nair: depends on model and sequence length. for a 4x A100 equivalent pool with moderate quantization, many customers see p95 in the 220–400 ms range for 512 tokens. we can share more specific runbook and the model benchmark sheet.
[04:29] Raj Patel: do you support automatic fallback to a cheaper model when capacity is constrained? that's something we like for graceful degradation.
[04:35] Jordan Lee: yes, smart routing supports fallback policies by model family or region. you can set prioritized model lists in rollout configs. if the primary is full, requests move to the next compatible variant. logs indicate when fallbacks occur.
[04:47] Maya Chen: good. observability — what are the integrations? we use Datadog + OpenTelemetry.
[04:52] Mateo Alvarez: we emit OTLP traces and expose Prometheus metrics. Datadog customers either ingest OTLP or use our metrics push. we also produce per-request JSON meta that includes model, tokens_in, tokens_out, and cost_estimate. these can be correlated to traces.
[05:08] Sofia Rivera: for compliance we need immutable audit trails for model inference decisions. can you provide long-term retention of request logs?
[05:15] Priya Nair: yes, retention is configurable as an enterprise add-on. Private deployments can keep logs in-situ; hosted logs can be exported to your cloud storage via a secure export job.
[05:24] Maya Chen: one more on architecture: we'd like to front Redwood with our existing gateway which handles auth and routing. is it okay to treat Redwood as a downstream and have one of your supported auth modes?
[05:34] Jordan Lee: absolutely. supported auth modes: API keys, mTLS, and signed JWT assertions from your IDP. the sidecar can also integrate with your gateway so you insert local auth.
[05:44] Raj Patel: raises a question around quotas again — if we have local gateway rate limiting plus Redwood quotas, is there a risk of double enforcement?
[05:50] Priya Nair: you'd typically implement the authoritative limit at one layer. our sidecar can act as the authoritative quota enforcer and let your gateway be permissive. we also expose a preflight endpoint so your gateway can query quota remaining to make smarter routing decisions.
[06:06] Evan Torres: about Private — if we go Private, what parts of the control plane remain with Redwood vs self-hosted?
[06:13] Priya Nair: in our Private mode, the control plane is customer-managed for critical paths: model manifests, KMS keys, audit logs. We still provide an ops console that can run inside your VPC. Redwood will assist with upgrades as part of the enterprise contract.
[06:26] Maya Chen: security deep-dive later is probably needed. we'll share our security questionnaire.
[06:30] Sofia Rivera: yes please. also want to validate any data exfil logic.
[06:34] Jordan Lee: totally. we'll send the security pack and an NDA'd SOC2 package if needed.
[06:38] Priya Nair: quick note on SDKs and adapters — we have official python and node SDKs, plus sample LangChain LLM wrapper and a LlamaIndex connector. typical migration is 1–2 dev days for a small team.
[06:49] Maya Chen: that sounds promising. can you run a small benchmark on our dataset? we can provide 20–50 sample requests that represent worst-case context length.
[06:58] Jordan Lee: yes — we recommend a 4-hour benchmark run on a dedicated pool. we'll need the request traces, token histograms, and the prompt set.
[07:07] Evan Torres: what's the cost model for that benchmark?
[07:11] Jordan Lee: we usually run an initial small benchmark complimentary; for full scale tests we may bill at cost if it requires reservation of GPUs — we'll clarify in the next email.
[07:20] Raj Patel: on deployment side, network egress costs are big for us. how do you recommend minimizing egress while keeping low latency?
[07:28] Priya Nair: options: private link so traffic stays in region; use the sidecar to consolidate requests and perform local caching; or Dedicated in your cloud region if you want the least egress. we'll include a cost/egress tradeoff matrix.
[07:41] Maya Chen: any existing customers with similar patterns? examples help.
[07:45] Mateo Alvarez: yes — a fintech customer used sidecar + dedicated pools and got 40% reduction in egress and 25% better p95. we'll anonymize details and share a case study.
[07:54] Sofia Rivera: circle back on RBAC — can we limit model access per environment? staging vs prod?
[07:59] Priya Nair: yes, model-level RBAC and per-environment namespaces are supported.
[08:05] Evan Torres: ok, let's recap.
[08:07] Jordan Lee: recap: 1) Redwood to share dedicated sizing and burst policy doc by 12/01. 2) Conflux will send sample traces, token histogram and LangChain snippets by 12/04. 3) we'll schedule a SE-led benchmark w/ dedicated pool week of 12/11. 4) Redwood to send security pack and KMS integration notes by 12/03.
[08:28] Maya Chen: that's right. thanks everyone. any final Qs?
[08:31] Raj Patel: nothing else from infra.
[08:33] Sofia Rivera: no. thanks.
[08:34] Jordan Lee: great — we'll follow up with an email with links to the sidecar repo, LangChain adapter, and the security docs. thanks all.
[08:42] meeting end: 16:57 UTC

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributions; filler words retained. references: sidecar repo (shortlink shared in follow-up), security pack (link to be sent), benchmark spreadsheet (will be shared).
